name: Pueraria mirifica (white kwao krua)
short: Case report: QT prolongation and repeated torsade de pointes in a woman with a long-QT gene variant. Japan: many reports of irregular vaginal bleeding and menstrual disorders with supplements.
text: Heart rhythm (case report): after taking an oestrogen-containing supplement derived from Pueraria mirifica, a 24-year-old woman developed marked QT prolongation and repeated torsade de pointes (a dangerous ventricular arrhythmia); she was found to carry the gene variant KCNQ1-T587M, which the title links to type 1 long QT syndrome, and the authors call it the first report of Pueraria mirifica-related acquired long QT syndrome. Oestrogen-like effects reported by consumers in Japan: a 2022 report says many adverse events, such as irregular vaginal bleeding and menstrual disorders, were reported from 2012 to 2017 in a Japanese system called PIO-NET with health foods containing Pueraria mirifica, which are sold with breast-enlarging or body-shaping claims, and that the Japanese government then labelled it a 'designated ingredient'; in that report's survey, almost half of users of foods containing it reported adverse events such as irregular vaginal bleeding and menstrual disorder. An online survey of Japanese women using supplements that claim oestrogen-like effects found that participants in their teens and 20s also used Pueraria mirifica and that, 'among them', 16.2% had experienced adverse events including irregular vaginal bleeding, breast swelling and pain, and heavy menstruation; the abstract does not make clear whether that figure refers to all young users or to Pueraria mirifica users only. These are consumer reports and surveys, which cannot prove cause. Trials (capsules or tablets by mouth): a 2018 systematic review of 8 studies in 309 menopausal women found adverse event rates (breast pain, vaginal spotting, dizziness) similar with Pueraria mirifica, conjugated equine oestrogen and placebo, but serum C-reactive protein (an inflammation marker) doubled; the reviewers rated the studies as having high risks of bias and low quality and called for robust pharmacovigilance. In a 24-week placebo-controlled trial in 71 healthy postmenopausal women, endometrial thickness did not change, no endometrial proliferation or hyperplasia was reported, there were no significant differences from placebo in adverse effects on breast tissue, blood counts or liver and kidney tests, and mild adverse effects occurred with both Pueraria mirifica and placebo. In an open study in 37 perimenopausal women, transient abnormal results, including anaemia and liver tests, occurred in a small number; in a double-blind study comparing two doses in 52 women after hysterectomy, no significant side effects were observed. Rats (animal data only): in Donryu rats, Pueraria mirifica increased uterine weight and mammary-gland cell proliferation, and after chemical carcinogens it significantly increased the incidence of mammary adenocarcinoma and the multiplicity of endometrial atypical hyperplasia; at higher doses it caused dilatation, haemorrhage and inflammation of the uterine wall. Product identity: a Japanese analysis found that some health food products sold as white kwao keur (Pueraria candollei var. mirifica) did not come from the labelled plant. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
